text: The Ozempic cliff: generic risks, opportunities and bottlenecks

The advent of Ozempic (semaglutide) generics in Canada, India and Brazil provides insights into the future of the diabesity market, with consequences for originators (Novo, Lilly, and other branded companies) and for generic companies, CDMOs and API/device suppliers.

We leverage MS's global footprint to gain insights into the impact of semaglutide generics across local markets. The arrival of generic versions of Novo's GLP-1 Ozempic (semaglutide) is set to drive the next shift in the diabetes and obesity markets, with the first countries a testing ground for the US and Europe. Following the expiration of market exclusivity, generics of Ozempic have been launched in India and Canada,

and the first generic should launch in Brazil in the coming weeks. We leverage granular data on sales, volume and market share of GLP-1s in India to get the first picture of a post-generic GLP-1 market. We also map the market formation in Brazil and Canada, where we expect to see sharp price erosion, volume expansion and the emergence of a 2-tier market with lower price semaglutide and higher price differentiated GLP-1+ medicines (Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and future innovative drugs).
We believe that insights on generic market formation in the first countries will provide investors with perspectives on how the global diabesity market will

continue to evolve. Following the market developments in these countries will provide investors with insights into how the US and European diabesity markets could evolve in the next wave of patent expiries in the early/mid-2030s. This will be key to assessing the outlook for branded obesity/diabetes drugs, starting with Lilly and Novo, but also for future innovative launches in the category from other originators (Amgen, Roche, AstraZeneca, Pfizer, Structure Therapeutics amongst others). We expect category winners to emerge within the generic industry, with generic companies leveraging global footprint and integrated supply chain more likely to capture the benefit of category volume expansion.

generics. text: Why does the first entry of generics constitute a key event in the GLP-1 / diabesity market? Following the expiration of market exclusivity after the end of the patent protection period, generic versions of semaglutide/Ozempic (Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 for diabetes) have been launched in India and Canada, and will launch in Brazil in the coming weeks; other countries will follow in the coming years with the largest markets (US and Europe) seeing generics entry in the early to mid 2030's. With the cost of manufacturing injectable GLP-1 such as Ozempic and Wegovy relatively low, competition from generics will lead to meaningful price erosion (e.g. >65% price reduction in Canada within the first year). This will have a direct impact on Novo Nordisk's existing GLP-1 franchise (\~75% of sales), with the company committed to leverage its manufacturing cost advantage to compete with generic makers on pricing in countries where market exclusivity has expired. Improved affordability of semaglutide should drive greater adoption of GLP-1 across countries, in particular in low-to-medium income countries where these drugs are mostly paid out-of-pocket, which should drive volume expansion for the GLP-1 category. We expect the emergence of a 2-tiered market in countries post-semaglutide patent expiry, with semaglutide becoming an affordable mass-market staple molecule, while oral GLP-1's and next-gen products (GLP-1+) from Lilly, Novo and new entrants (Amgen, Roche, AstraZeneca, Pfizer, Structure Therapeutics amongst others) should compete in a higher value, branded segment.

Why is there a debate on the semaglutide generics supply chain? Semaglutide is a peptide drug, and hence not a traditional small molecule like a statin that is easy to copy and manufacture at scale. The success of Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly's injectable GLP-1 franchises Ozempic/Wegovy (semaglutide) and Mounjaro/Zepbound (tirzepatide) led to shortages in the US between 2021 and 2024 and limited availability globally. The key bottleneck in the manufacturing process of these drugs were on the Fill-and-Finish (F&F) process, i.e. turning the active ingredient into a sterile liquid and packaging it into a ready-to-use pen or device. Fill-and-Finish requires highly controlled cleanroom space to minimise contamination risk, requires FDA inspection/approval, and building new F&F capacity takes 3+ years. Novo and Lilly invested dozens of US\$ billions in building more capacity for F&F, including Novo's acquisition of three F&F sites from Catalent in 2024. Since then, the combination of manufacturing optimisation and new F&F sites coming online have released the manufacturing bottleneck on injectables, and Novo Nordisk and Lilly have been able to supply the US market and expand the geographic reach of their injectable franchise. However, there is an investor debate on whether generic makers will be able to replicate the supply chain of Novo and Lilly and manufacture enough injectable generics to address the growing demand stimulated by improved affordability. Our analysis suggests that while there is plenty of capacity scaling in China for the API (active pharmaceutical ingredient), the situation is less clear for F&F capacity, and generic makers will likely either need to invest to build capacity in coming years to address the largest markets (US and Europe), or introduce formulations where F&F is less of a bottleneck (e.g. multi-dose vials rather than pen/autoinjectors).

Peptide vs. small molecules, why does it matter in the GLP-1 oral pill battle and in the debate around the generics impact? The answer resides in convenience and scalability. Novo's oral GLP-1 is a reformulation of semaglutide, a peptide, into a pill form.

Peptides are a type of molecule which usually cannot be taken orally as they are mostly broken down by stomach enzymes before they can reach their target in the body. To get around this limitation, Novo Nordisk leveraged a formulation technology (SNAC) allowing for improved peptide absorption, but with two drawbacks: 1) the need to take the pill in the morning on an empty stomach and not eat/drink/take other pills for 30 minutes; and 2) the need for a very large quantity of API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) to compensate for a poor absorption through the oral route. Indeed, the pill formulation of semaglutide requires 63-73x more API than the injection for the maintenance dose of equivalent strength of the injectable formulation. This increases manufacturing cost but also limits the scalability of the pill, limiting Novo's reach to the US and some select OUS markets. This also limits the ability of generic manufacturers to scale generic copies of Novo's oral pill. In contrast, Lilly's oral pill Foundayo (orfoglipron) is a true small molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist which is easier to manufacture at large scale and does not have the fasting/food/drink restriction of the semaglutide oral pill. We note however that cross-trial comparison favours semaglutide in terms of efficacy (weight loss of \~12% for Foundayo at week 72 vs. 16-17% for Wegovy Pill at week 64).
How does the generic debate feed into MS global obesity model

forecasts? In our most recent global report on the GLP-1 broadening (see Biopharma: Obesity Medications: Tracking the GLP-1 'Unlock' (7 Apr 2026)), we framed our expectations for the global GLP-1 market (combining branded and generic drugs) and forecast \$142bn obesity market in a base case (assuming that the branded market retains a higher value through differentiation and market segmentation), and \$100bn in a bear base (including pricing pressure and generic competition). We separately forecast \$49bn market for GLP-1 diabetes in 2035, leading to a global GLP-1 market of \$190bn in our base case (from a \~\$90bn market in 2026). Insights from market dynamics in Canada in particular will inform our view on how other developed markets will evolve in terms of price, penetration/volume, and growth of the oral and innovative branded segments.

text: 1) We believe generic makers will have no issue sourcing API, but fill-and-finish (F&F) could be a bottleneck

Our global deep dive on the emerging supply chain for generic semaglutide (Ozempic) suggests that producing enough API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) will not be an issue for injectable formulations, although scaling supply for the oral pill formulation will remain a challenge. The API requirements for semaglutide injectable is modest, with 10 to 15 tons of API enough to supply >100m patients with Ozempic or Wegovy low dose annually. The Chinese API industry has already set up large chemical synthesis manufacturing capacity for semaglutide API with credible local players already building towards multi-ton capacity. Our analysis of the FDA import data suggests that 40% of semaglutide shipments into the US (ex-Novo/Catalent) over 2024-2026 originated from 5 Chinese suppliers (JYMed, Sinopep-Allsino, Hybio Pharmaceuticals, Fujian Genohope, Aurisco), with a large proportion of shipments likely supplying the US compounding industry. However, supplying a generic oral pill version of semaglutide will be challenging even with multi-ton capacity, with Ozempic/Wegovy pills requiring \~63-73x more API than the equivalent strength in injectable formulation at maintenance. We note that Eli Lilly's Foundayo (oral GLP-1 pill) is a true small molecule and not a peptide, and hence the company will be able to scale globally.

However, fill-and-finish (F&F) capacity could potentially emerge as a bottleneck for injectable generics. While pen/cartridge manufacturers continue to invest and ramp-up capacity and could be integrated into semaglutide generic supply chains, the situation is less clear for F&F capacity, which was also the bottleneck faced by Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly when ramping-up injectable supply over 2021-2024 before their large investments in F&F (and the Catalent acquisition for Novo) progressively resolved the issue. Investments to address the demand for generic semaglutide have started (e.g. OneSource capacity increase to supply some of the first approved generics), but disclosures from generic companies and CDMOs on F&F capacity allocated to generic semaglutide remain scarce. We believe Canada, India and Brazil are likely to be a testing ground for generic makers to assess market dynamics, and positive ROI in these geographies is likely to trigger larger investments in F&F to address larger markets in Europe (LOE 2031) and the US (LOE from 2032). The launch of vial formulations (three on the market in India and likely to be replicated elsewhere), which are cheaper and easier to manufacture could also be a workaround to the F&F bottleneck, as seen previously with the launch of vials by compounders in the US and Brazil.
2) Generic market formation in Canada, India and Brazil indicate sharp price erosion, volume expansion and emergence of a 2-tier market

The market formation has started in Canada, the second largest GLP-1 market; we expect steep price erosion. Canada will be a key battleground for Novo and generic makers, as it provides the best blueprint for what could happen in the US and Europe in the early/mid-2030s. We estimate that Canada was a \$2-2.5bn GLP-1 market in 2025, including \$1.5-2bn sales for semaglutide. Dr Reddy's and Apotex have launched the first two generics in the market; the launch of a third generic in coming months (likely from either Sandoz, Teva, Taro or Aspen) would trigger a mandatory 65% price cut on branded price, leading price to decline from \~\$150/month pre-generic to \~\$50/month before the end of 2026. We expect pricing pressure to continue in 2027 as generic makers compete for market share, and we forecast the Canada semaglutide market to stabilise at \$800-900m through a combination of volume growth and price decline, with Novo retaining a \~\$250m tail.

With the entry of generics, the India market for GLP-1 could scale up from \$123m in CY25 to \~\$1bn in CY30. 13 companies have launched 26 generics of semaglutide since March 2026 across several presentations (single-dose, multi-dose, vials and pills) at price points from \~\$15/month for vials to \$60-70/month for more premium injectable offerings. Two players have launched oral tablets (generic Rybelsus) in the 3mg, 7mg and 14mg strength priced \~\$1-\$2.4 per tablet. We expect more launches to enter the market in the coming months. Semaglutide volumes have increased >6x between February and April, with generics already capturing >80% of semaglutide volume, and key players starting to emerge (Torrent, Lupin, DRL, Zydus, and SunPharma). Post generics launch, Eli Lilly continues to be the largest player in value through premium pricing with Mounjaro (GLP-GIP). LLY noted on 1Q26 earnings that the recent launch of generic semaglutide has had a halo effect on the overall GLP-1 market, and Mounjaro has actually grown 10% in the face of generics (see HERE). Novo Nordisk value and volumes have remained flat in absolute at a low level, with the market expansion driven by generics. We forecast the market to continue to grow from \~\$123m in CY25 to \~\$1bn in CY30, with a segmentation between mass-market volume growth for semaglutide (likely dominated by fewer scaled generics players with supply chain integration, device capabilities, and distribution strength) and a premium market likely dominated by Eli Lilly's Mounjaro.

Brazil's first generic version of semaglutide has been approved; we expect prices to decline followed by market expansion to the benefit of generics, and Eli Lilly in the branded segment. The first generic from local manufacturer EMS was approved in Brazil on 26 May, with a launch expected in June/July and potentially further generic manufacturers to follow (17 generic filings in process). Brazil's branded GLP-1 market is currently underpenetrated, with current prices (\$160-320/month) restricting branded GLP-1 access to higher-income patients in the context of a largely out-of-pocket market; elevated price has also led to the formation of a large compounded/unauthorized import market potentially as large as 3-4x the official market. We forecast the introduction of semaglutide generics to drive down costs (down to \~\$60/month by 2027) and increase penetration, growing the Brazil GLP-1 market from \~\$2bn in 2026 to \~\$8bn in 2028. We expect generic makers (EMS, Hyperia, and global competitors) to be the main beneficiaries at the expense of Novo's franchise, while Eli Lilly should continue to dominate the branded segment with Mounjaro. Risks to our Brazil market forecast could come from further expansion of the compounded/black market.
3) Stock conclusions: prefer Lilly over Novo, prefer generics companies will global reach and integrated supply chains, prefer scaled API suppliers

We expect LLY's (OW rated) franchise to be more insulated from generic pressure given: (1) Differentiation of Mounjaro (Tirzepatide; GLP-GIP) vs. Semaglutide (GLP) based on head-to-head Ph3 data in obesity and T2D, (2) a portfolio of pipeline drugs with novel mechanisms of action such as Retatrutide (GLP-GIP-glucagon) and Eloralintide (selective amylin), and (3) a small molecule oral GLP-1 pill in Foundayo (notably this is not a peptide like Novo's oral Wegovy, which constrains scalability as we discuss within). LLY's CSO recently noted that Retatrutide could also represent a "workhorse" for obesity patients with lower BMI, as the low dose Ph3 data compare favorably to Tirzepatide with respect to weight loss, tolerability and time of dose escalation (see HERE). We model LLY incretin franchise sales growing from \~\$60bn in 2026 to \~\$100bn in 2035. See our note from earlier this year Tracking the GLP-1 'Unlock.'

We expect Novo Nordisk to be under pressure in post-LOE markets. We expect Canada to be the bellwether for future developed market dynamics over coming years; specifically, the extent to which price and volume competition in the semaglutide franchise leads to an erosion of Novo's Wegovy/Ozempic sales. We see some scope for Novo to partially compensate through its Wegovy Pill and through innovation. On Wegovy Pill, script trends in the US YTD have been encouraging (although we are waiting to see prescriptions trends holding through the summer and escalation to highest doses) but we believe the API requirement will limit Novo's ability execute on a broad ex-US launch (unlike LLY with Foundayo). On innovation, CagriSema (GLP-1/amylin) launch in 2027 will be a first step to partially protect the franchise in the US, but we see more potential from the cagrilintide mono (amylin, potential launch in 2028), zenagamtide/amycretin subcut (GLP-1/amylin 2029-2030) and more importantly zenagamtide oral (2030), which carries the highest differentiation potential in our view. At this stage, we see less potential for Novo's triple agonists, which will only come to market next decade and 5+ years after Lilly's retatrutide. Therefore, with key new launches skewed to 2028-2030+, we see a risk for Novo's diabetes/obesity franchise to struggle between inexpensive semaglutide generics and innovation from Lilly and other branded players, and we see consensus' forecasts for \$23bn sales for semaglutide in 2033 as likely at risk (MSe \$16bn).
We highlight potential beneficiaries amongst generic makers / CDMOs / suppliers.

text: Supply chain formation for generic semaglutide
The emergence of a global semaglutide market will depend on the ability of generic makers to establish and scale supply chains comparable to Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly.

The shortage of Ozempic/Wegovy/Mounjaro over 2021-2024 has illustrated the complexity in building and scaling-up supply chains to meet global demand for injectable GLP-1. As innovative and generic competition continues to drive a moderation in prices over the coming years, we expect GLP-1 penetration in diabetes and obesity to increase, leading to meaningful volume expansion. Therefore, generic makers seeking to enter and expand global GLP-1 markets with generic semaglutide products will also need to establish and scale supply chains including API, pen/devices and fill-and-finish.
API considerations: likely manageable for injectables, challenging for orals
Semaglutide API requirements depend on formulation, ranging from relatively low API quantity needed for Ozempic 1mg to large volumes required for oral formulations of Ozempic/Wegovy.

For patients this implies an API requirement of 52mg/patient/week or 104mg/patient/week depending on the maintenance dose.

- Wegovy Injectable (125mg/patient/year to 374mg/patient/year for high dose): Wegovy maintenance dose is 2.4mg/week (standard), to 7.2mg/week (Wegovy High Dose). This implies an API requirement of 125mg/patient/year Wegovy standard or 374mg/patient/year for Wegovy high dose.

- Wegovy Pill (up to 9.125g/patient/year for a patient on maintenance): the daily doses for Wegovy Pill are 1.5mg for the starting dose (one month) / 4mg (one month), 9mg (one month) / 25mg (maintenance). At the maintenance dose of 25mg, Wegovy pill requires 9.125g of API/patient/year, 73x more API than Wegovy injectable 2.4mg and 24x more API than Wegovy HD. We note that the proportion of patients ramping to high dose is still a debate currently considering the recent launch of the pill.

This would simplify the supply chain with Ozempic Pill and Wegovy Pill being effectively the same drug with the same formulation and the same doses (only differing in brand and indication).

text: API manufacturing: hybrid recombinant / synthetic (Novo) vs. full chemical synthesis (Generics)

Semaglutide can be produced through a semi-recombinant / semi-synthetic approach (Novo) or through chemical synthesis (most generics). Novo's manufacturing route can be described as semi-recombinant / semi-synthetic, with the peptide backbone manufactured through a yeast-based RNA recombinant method, and chemistry introducing additional modifications. In contrast, many generic developers are producing the API through chemical peptide synthesis, usually Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis (SPPS) or hybrid SPPS and Liquid-Phase Peptide Synthesis (LPPS), followed by side-chain modification and extensive purification. When considering applications from generic makers, regulators focus on whether the final API is the same and whether route-specific impurities are controlled.

The semi-recombinant manufacturing is more expensive to establish (high initial CAPEX requirement) but is more efficient at scale, while the chemical synthesis route has lower barriers to entry but also lower yield at large scale. The key advantages of Novo's approach (yeast-based peptide backbone) is efficiency and better opportunity for yield optimisation at large scale, but building capacity is more capital intensive and takes longer. This is not an easy route for generic makers as it requires biologics/fermentation infrastructure, technology and know-how. By contrast, the chemical synthesis route is faster to develop and the manufacturing chain is more flexible/modulable, but does not have the same yield optimisation opportunity compared to the semi-recombinant route.
We expect API providers and generics makers to be able to supply the API for the injectable formulation at global scale, but producing sufficient API for the pill will be a challenge.

The API required to supply injectable semaglutide is modest; on a rough estimate, the generic industry could supply >100m patients at the global level with only 10-15 tons of API. The API required to supply at large scale the global market with Ozempic 1mg/week (corresponding to the 4mg pen already launched by Dr Reddy's and Apotex in Canada) appears manageable; with 52kg of semaglutide API enough to supply 1m patients at the maintenance dose. The API requirements escalate with the higher doses of semaglutide, with 374kg of API required to supply 1m patients on the Wegovy High Dose pen at maintenance dose. Assuming that the generic industry will focus the generic opportunity on Ozempic and Wegovy, the combined industry could supply >100m patients with 10 to 15 tons of API. We believe the China generic makers, API suppliers and CDMO companies already have significant API capacity and will be able to ramp up to the level required to supply global markets over the coming years.

We believe API and formulation technology considerations are likely to prevent generic manufacturers from manufacturing semaglutide pill generics at scale, although we note that some companies have already launched oral pill (Rybelsus generics) in India. The API requirements for Ozempic Pill and Wegovy Pill are much larger than for the injectable formulations. As an example, to supply 1 million patients on the maintenance dose assuming 100% compliance over a year, 9.125 tons of API are required for Wegovy Pill, 73x more than for Wegovy 2.4mg (125kg for 1m patients on maintenance) and 24x more than for Wegovy High Dose (374kg for 1m patients on maintenance). Additionally, on top of pure API capacity, generic makers would also need to match Novo's updated SNAC technology in terms of API absorption through the oral route. However, we note that generic maker Torrent Pharmaceuticals has launched a generic version of Rybelsus (Semalix), and Dr Reddy's has launched an oral version (Obeda), although supply capacity is unknown. Several other pill generic projects are in development for ex-US countries.

text: China has accumulated significant semaglutide API capacity over the years, and is the world's biggest supplier of APIs. China's CDMOs (focusing on novel drugs) and API makers (focusing on generic APIs and formulations) have readied substantial capacity in anticipation of generic launches in China and overseas, although not all producers are choosing to allocate capacity, and commentaries from listed manufacturers suggest a wide range of quality for the semaglutide API.

Partly a result of regulatory loophole: The compound patent for semaglutide patent was filed in March 2006. Under the 20-year patent term set by the WTO, it was set to expire in March 2026, which is what happened in China on March 20, 2026. In the US and EU, however, Novo has pushed out the expiry dates to 2031-2033, leveraging the patent term extension mechanisms there.

\- In the US, the Patent Term Adjustments and Patent Term Extensions under the Hatch-Waxman Act offer extensions to compensate for time lost during the regulatory review process. These pushed the expiries of the compound patent (US8129343) and the patent for use of long-acting GLP-1 peptides for diabetes/obesity (US10335462) to December 2031 and June 2033.
\- In Europe, the Supplementary Protection Certificates serve the same purpose, extending patent expiries by up to 5 years. This pushed semaglutide patent protection up to March 2031.

\- In China, however, no such mechanism existed prior to June 2021, when the government introduced a similar extension mechanism modeled on US/EU's. Semaglutide (Ozempic) was first approved in China in April, 2021 for the diabetes indication, thus narrowly missing the enactment of the extension pathway. Application of the law is not retroactive either.

Why is China uniquely positioned to manufacture peptides at scale? With the above as background, we distill the following reasons why China has accumulated so much semaglutide capacity, or peptide capacity for that matter.

1. Pre-existing position as the world's API factory: About 30% of the world's API capacity is located in China. In the 20+ years since joining the WTO, China's cost advantages, vast pool of chemistry talent, and a willingness to start from the lower-end of the pharmaceutical value chain have catapulted China to a leadership position in API, with 40+ export-oriented listed API companies (see our primer). As experts in synthetic chemistry, many have developed solid-phase peptide synthesis capacities.
2. Operating at lower cost: This advantage stems from lower labor costs and raw material prices (note). This positions China as an attractive service provider to more cost conscious customers.

3. Semaglutide's early patent expiry: A delayed enactment of the patent term extension mechanism led to an expiry date (April 2027) that is 4-5 years ahead of those in US/EU. Coupled with a vast Chinese diabetes population (\~12% of the adult population, source), this created a powerful incentive for Chinese producers to invest in semaglutide API capacity. Some are also eyeing the export markets of Canada, Brazil, and India. As of Q1'26, 74 Chinese companies had obtained FDA DMF registrations for semaglutide API supply, while in China, 13 had filed applications for API supply, with none approved yet. And as showed in Exhibit 33, 10+ companies have submitted applications for biosimilars, but the frontrunners are being held up by the China-Switzerland Free Trade Agreement (CSFTA) (news).

4. A vast and under-penetrated domestic market: There were 148 million adult diabetics in China as of 2024. Current barriers to uptake in the prescription channel include low levels of reimbursement, needle phobia (see our survey here), and a gray market which is under increased regulatory crackdowns. In other words, China's API makers could pivot either way: China or overseas.

5. Mastery of SPPS (solid-phase peptide synthesis): SPPS is a widely used lab technique for chemically creating peptides. It strings together amino acids one by one on an insoluble resin bead. Semaglutide is a complex 31-amino acid peptide with a fatty acid side chain, making large-scale, high-purity production technically challenging. Chinese manufacturers have successfully mastered the core technologies for large-scale, high-purity production of long-chain peptides like semaglutide, including technological mastery and process maturity that presents significant technical barriers to entry. A number of
leading manufacturers have achieved ton-scale mass production of semaglutide, with some production lines designed for 10-ton scale.

6. Significant capex in peptide infrastructure: China's leading CDMOs in the TIDES (peptides + oligonucleotides) space have deployed significant capital to capacity buildup. WuXi AppTec is the leader, with SPPS capacity reaching 100,000L by 3Q25 and a projected increase of 30% within 2026 to 130,000L. In 2023 alone, its TIDES business produced more than 15 tons of peptide APIs and intermediates (on 50 preclinical to commercial stage projects). Asymchem had 45,000L of SPPS capacity by end-2025, and expects to expand this to 69,000L within 2026 (+53%). Medtide, a pure-play CDMO specializing in TIDES, has an annual production capacity of over one ton. Other suppliers include Pharmaron, Jiuyuan Genetic, and Sihuan. As of end-2024, Sihuan had two sets of 12,000L fermentation systems dedicated to semaglutide production.

7. Government support: According to commentary (link) by Caplin Point Labs, supportive policies by the Chinese government have created a highly competitive and fragmented supplier base of 500-600 companies in the biosimilar/generic space, versus 7-10 large companies in India.

8. Sizable export markets: What originally incentivized the domestic supplier base was China's own generic market (now delayed to April 2027) and the compounding market in the US. Following restrictions in the US on the latter, Chinese suppliers have since pivoted towards other generic markets in addition to China's, e.g. Canada, Brazil, and India.

Quantifying the domestic base for semaglutide API manufacturing: CDMOs and API makers alike have ramped up significantly their peptide capacities. As of Q1'26, the US FDA had granted 90 DMFs (Drug Master Files) to suppliers for the semaglutide API. Of those, 74 were Chinese companies (82%), followed by 8 for India (9%). Despite a large number of Chinese suppliers for semaglutide, only a few are on FDA's Green List. Medtide (3880-HK) has disclosed that it is one qualified supplier - "The Group's semaglutide API was included on the Green List of U.S. FDA Import Alert 66-80, designating it as eligible for entry into the United States without detention. This recognition follows FDA's evaluation of the Group's manufacturing facilities and quality systems, and reflects the Group's compliance with U.S. cGMP requirements." The Green List comprises foreign manufacturers whose facilities and products have been evaluated by the FDA and comply with current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) requirements. In terms of peptide capacity, the largest suppliers in China are CDMOs WuXi AppTec and Asymchem, although these companies service mainly novel drug contracts. A number of suppliers have ton-scale annual capacities for peptide APIs, but not all have significant plans for semaglutide. We set out the potential semaglutide suppliers below. JYMed, Hybio, and Jiangsu Sinopep-Allsino are openly committed to semaglutide API supplies. Medtide has ton-scale peptide capacity but has not commented on an intent to capture the semaglutide market (although FDA shipment data suggest that the company is exporting batches to the US through its subsidiary China Peptide Company). For now, it is focused on novel drug development.

text: Fill-and-finish could be an initial bottleneck for the generics industry
The device requirement based on the multi-dose pen is 13 pens/patient/year. For

Ozempic, Novo Nordisk is using the fletouch pen (4 weekly doses in a pen) globally. For Wegovy, Novo Nordisk is using the fletouch pen ex-US and a single-use weekly pen in the US (52 pens/patient/year), although the company is waiting for the approval of the Wegovy multi-dose pen in the US in Q2'26. Therefore, the pen volume requirement for generic maker will likely remain at 13 pen/patient/year across geographies with a multi-dose pen.
Vial formulation can offer lower costs and higher flexibility and could help with

supply chain bottlenecks. Ozempic and Wegovy are currently only available in pre-filled pen formulations; however Novo is working on introducing a vial formulation of Wegovy in 2026. The vial formulation (vial + a separate needle and syringe) is an important consideration as it allows for lower manufacturing costs, and more importantly is a way to overcome potential supply chain bottleneck on the pen/device and associated F&F capacity. We note that three generics makers have already launched vial formulations in India, with additional companies expressing an interest in the formulation. In Canada, at least one company (Vimy Pharma) is also planning to sell a vial formulation. We note that grey market / compounded GLP-1 in the US and Brazil are mostly marketed through a vial formulation as well.

Novo's total F&F/device capacity is not known, however we estimate that Ozempic and Wegovy global sales in 2025 corresponded to an equivalent of\~128m multi-dose pens annually; we forecast \~138m equivalent multi-dose pen to support 2026 sales. For Ozempic, we estimate that Novo sold \~100m pens in 2025; we used international sales (\$5.8bn in 2025) and assumed an average price/pen of \$85 leading to 69m pens for International operations. For the US, we used the TRx number (30m in 2025). We note that in March 2025, Novo indicated that 7m patients worldwide were being treated with Ozempic, which would correspond to 91m annualised pen sales in March 2025, consistent with our estimate of \~100m for 2025. For Wegovy, we do a similar calculation assuming \$250/month in IO leading to 17m multi-dose pens. In the US, Wegovy is sold as single-dose pen (4 pen/month vs. 1 pen/month for the multi-dose), so 13m scripts in 2025 correspond to \~51m pens, leading to a total number of pens at 68m. Converting the Wegovy US into equivalent multi-dose pen volume would lead to total multi-dose pen volume of 30m pens for Wegovy in 2025. Therefore, we estimate that to address Novo's current semaglutide global market, \~128m multi-dose pens would be required.

text: Commentary from generics and CDMOs on pen / fill-and-finish capacity are scarce and existing capacity in the industry is difficult to assess, but we believe that more investment will be needed to supply globally. The most vocal F&F company working with generic manufacturers is OneSource Specialty Pharma, which is providing fill-and-finish services for Dr Reddy's (Canada) and Apotex (Canada and US). The company is currently executing on a \$100m investment plan to scale its total drug-device cartridge capacity from 40 million to 220 million units/year, with the expansion driven by anticipated demand for semaglutide generic F&F across global markets (only part of the capacity is allocated to semaglutide). Gland Pharma is another example of a company investing to build F&F capacity to serve the generic industry, with the company planning to commercialize around 20 million pens and cartridges for GLP-1 products by fiscal year 2027, and has invested to increase its total cartridge fill-and-finish capacity to 140 million units in 2026. We note that some of the largest F&F suppliers (e.g. Thermo Fisher, Simtra and Vetter) are unlikely to work with semaglutide generics makers as they tend to reserve their capacity for higher margins innovator/complex projects.

Commentary from companies involved in pen/cartridge/device manufacturing suggest growing investments and a ramp-up in pen capacity. Looking at comments from pen/ device manufacturers, Shaily Engineering Plastics (supplying the pen for Dr Reddy's Canada generic and Apotex US and Canada generics) recently integrated a 25 million pen capacity line dedicated to semaglutide. The company also announced an investment in a new facility in Abu Dhabi to produce 75m pens; and expect to reach a total pen capacity of 150m annually by March 2028 (although not all the capacity will be dedicated to semaglutide generics). The main pen/device manufacturers such as SHL medical, Ypsomed, Medmix, Nemera, Gerresheimer, BD, Schott Pharma, Phillips Medisize, etc. also offer pen/ cartridges for GLP-1 supply chains and are likely to be integrated into generics F&F supply chains. Most of these companies have announced capacity expansion plans (often >\$100m) at least partially driven by demand for GLP-1 therapies.

As an example, Stevanato (covered by Kallum Titchmarsh) provides drug delivery systems for GLP-1. GLP-1 revenue accounted for approximately 19%–20% of STVN's total company revenue, growing more than 50% compared with 2024. We estimate approximately 90%

STVN's GLP-1 business is branded, with roughly 10% coming from players other than the two largest branded manufacturers (Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly). The Nexa syringe was STVN's fastest growing product in 2025, driven primarily by GLP-1 demand. The company's strategy is to be present across both originators and biosimilars, noting that historically when a product goes off-patent, approximately 70% of revenue stays with the originator and 30% moves to biosimilars.

We estimate the existing GLP-1 market in Canada at \~US\$2-2.5bn, of which \~US\$1.5-2bn for semaglutide. Novo Nordisk reported \~US\$1.15bn sales for semaglutide in Canada in 2024 (US\$1bn for Ozempic and US\$150m for Wegovy). While Novo did not disclose semaglutide Canada sales in 2025, we estimate that sales were \~US\$1.6bn. This is consistent with the Dr Reddy's management estimate of Canada's existing semaglutide market of \~US\$1.8bn based on IQVIA data. Including Mounjaro sales (undisclosed, launched in November 2023, full supply availability in May 2025), we estimate the Canada pre-LOE market is \~US\$2-2.5bn.

We see Canada as a blueprint for how market dynamics could evolve in the US and Europe after LOE. Novo Nordisk management indicated that India is not an appropriate blueprint for other countries. One key reason is the under-development of the branded GLP-1 market ahead of generic launch, with only \~US\$50m of combined sales in India for Wegovy/Ozempic due to a combination of supply limitation (Wegovy launched in June 2025 and Ozempic only launched in December 2025, although Rybelsus was launched in 2022) and affordability barriers. Therefore, generic makers have entered India before the branded market could be established, forcing Novo Nordisk to cut prices to remain competitive in the context of generic launches. The second key point is the average income differential between India and the Western market making affordability and price a more acute focus in the country. The third key point is the more intense price competition from a large number of local players approved in India (13+ companies approved at IP expiry in the country). In comparison, Canada is much more comparable to the US and Europe in terms of regulatory requirements, average income and maturity of the branded GLP-1 market (Canada is the second largest GLP-1 market in the world).

Dr Reddy's and Apotex products were the first two semaglutide generics approved in Canada. Both companies received approval for a multi-dose 2mg and 4mg pen (corresponding to the 1.0mg/weekly Ozempic dose) and are approved only for the diabetes indication. The API for both products is manufactured through solid-phase synthetic chemistry (i.e. purely chemical process vs. Novo's hybrid biologic/chemical process). Dr Reddy's (approved 28 April, launched 16 May 2026) generic API is produced in-house. Apotex (approved 1 May, launched 14 May 2026) generic was developed in partnership with Orbicular Pharmaceutical Technologies; while the source of the API is unknown, we believe it is likely supplied by the Orbicular CMO network. The fill-and-finish for both Apotex and Dr Reddy's is handled by OneSource with device components provided by Shaily Engineering Plastics. The Apotex semaglutide generic (developed and manufactured with the same partners) also cleared tentative approval in the US.

Hims & Hers (covered by Craig Hettenbach) has partnered with Apotex to replicate the successful consumer-led approach taken in the US in Canada. H&H has announced the marketing of Apotex' generic through its platform for weight loss, despite the generic label indication being restricted to T2D. H&H offers treatment options starting at 149 CAD/month (US\$107/month) and follows the company's acquisition of Livewell, which was announced in December 2025. Livewell was founded in 2023 as a telehealth platform for weight loss, smoking cessation and sexual health and this acquisition was specifically aimed to align with the timeline of generic semaglutide availability in Canada. H&H press release indicates: Generic semaglutide is authorized for sale by Health Canada for the management of Type 2 diabetes. It may be prescribed off-label for weight management in a licensed healthcare provider's sole clinical judgment. Hims & Hers Canada Inc. does not currently offer access to treatment services for Type 2 diabetes. We remain Equal-weight on HIMS on a balanced risk/reward, with pressure on margins and decelerating core growth vs. potential upside in international growth and new category ramps (see Higher revenue guidance comes with a cost, as EBITDA is cut on weaker margins).

We expect the price of Ozempic in the public reimbursement channel to decline from \~US\$150/pen (depending on the region) to US\$70-80 in the near term, then \~US\$50 after a 3rd generic entry. The launch of a 3rd generic in Canada will trigger a price cut for all Ozempic generics in the reimbursed channels. Generic public reimbursement/list prices in Canada are set through the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance (pCPA) Tiered Pricing Framework for generics. When two generics are launched, the generic price is set to 50% of the brand reference price; when a third generic is launched, this triggers an automatic reimbursement/list-price tier change and the generic price is set at 35% of the brand reference price (for an injectable). While Novo Nordisk is not required to lower the price of branded Ozempic to the level of generics, a substantial price cut is likely for the drug to remain competitive against generics. We also note that while private plans in Canada do not have to follow the pCPA price, many do, effectively leading to a spillover of the public price into the private market.

Health Canada is currently reviewing generics from four other generic makers, with additional companies expected to file in coming months. In addition to the two approved generics from Apotex and Dr Reddy's, Health Canada is currently reviewing seven additional generics, of which three are additional filings from Apotex, and the other four are generics from Sandoz, Teva, Taro and Aspen. Aspen indicated that they expect approval between May and September 2026; Sandoz expect approval in the second half of 2026; Teva and Taro have not commented. Three additional companies are also developing a generic of semaglutide in Canada but have not yet filed according to Health Canada disclosures: PharmaTher (targeting approval in 2026), Biocon, and Canadian company Vimy Pharma, which is seeking to bring to market a vial generic manufactured by partners in Canada.

text: Scale of generic entry: Patent expiry triggered the entry of approximately 13+ generic players, with a 70–80% price drop. Generic semaglutide became available for as little as \$14 per month (approximately Rs 1,290).

Backward integration and scale: Initially most companies are importing the APIs. Few companies like DRL and Sunpharma are investing in full supply chain control, producing semaglutide API in-house and rapidly scaling production capacity. Indian CDMOs, including OneSource Specialty, are undertaking significant scale-up initiatives, targeting a \~4–5× increase in output by 2027 (e.g. Dr. Reddy's \~7mn pens in 2026 to >40mn pens by FY28 with F&F managed by OneSource). As per its FY25 Annual Report, OneSource is expanding cartridge manufacturing capacity from 40mn in FY25 to approximately 220mn by FY28.
Indian generic companies have pursued different API sourcing strategies:

list_items: - Dr. Reddy's Laboratories (DRL): The most notable example of full backward integration. DRL produces semaglutide API entirely in-house, with finished product manufacturing carried out by its manufacturing partner, OneSource Specialty Pharma Limited. DRL expects its semaglutide capacity to be around 6–7mn pens in CY2026, with FY28 capacity potentially exceeding 40mn.

- Torrent Pharma: Oral formulations are developed in-house, with API for both Semalix and Sembolic sourced from DRL. In injectables, the outsourcing model varies by product; Semalix pre-filled pens are sourced from DRL, while Symbolix pens are sourced from Zydus.
- Sunpharma: Sunpharma manufactures the semaglutide API on its own. The pre-filled pens for Noveltreat and Sematrinity are manufactured in Europe by leading global pharmaceutical device suppliers.
- Lupin: Partnered with Galenicum (a Spanish company) for finished formulations,

text: with Galenicum overseeing development, manufacturing, and supply, while Lupin handles regulatory submissions and commercialization across 23 countries.

list_items: - Shilpa Medicare: Developing both synthetic and semisynthetic API for semaglutide, with API validation batches ongoing and formulation development (both injectable and oral solid) completed.
- MSN Laboratories: Has vertically integrated semaglutide production, manufacturing both the API and the pen device in-house.
- Biocon: Describes itself as "vertically integrated" in semaglutide, supplying to Ajanta Pharma (India) for marketing in 26 countries.

- Cipla: On October 23, 2025, Lilly and Cipla signed a marketing and distribution agreement for a second brand of tirzepatide in India. Cipla launched Yurpeak (tirzepatide) on December 10, 2025, making it the second brand of Lilly's tirzepatide available in the Indian market, alongside Mounjaro.

- Emcure Pharma: Launched Poviztra (semaglutide injection) in India on December 22, 2025, under an exclusive partnership with Novo Nordisk, becoming the first Indian company to distribute and commercialise a second semaglutide brand for weight management.

- Abbott India: In February 2026, Abbott and Novo Nordisk partnered to market and distribute semaglutide (globally known as Ozempic) in India, with Abbott commercialising it as Extensor to expand access to advanced diabetes care.

text: \- Divi's Labs (manufactures for innovator): The company currently has the largest Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis (SPPS) scale (i.e. multiple \~3,000L reactors) in India. It manufactures fragments and amino acids for SPPS peptide drugs.

\- One Source Specialty: The company is a pure-play specialty pharmaceutical CDMO focused on complex drug-device combination (DDC) products. It does not manufacture semaglutide API but it provides end-to-end formulation, fill-and-finish, and device assembly services to pharma partners who bring their own API.

\- Anthem Biosciences: Anthem is the most backward-integrated semaglutide API manufacturer in India, manufacturing both the fermentation fragment (P29 precursor) and the chemical synthesis steps in-house making it one of the only companies in India to do so. This gives it a significant cost advantage to compete against Chinese API suppliers.

\- Shaily Engineering: Shaily Engineering Plastics is a drug delivery device manufacturer which designs, develops, and manufactures pen injectors and auto-injectors for semaglutide. It does not manufacture API or formulation. Its proprietary platforms include ShailyPen Neo (spring-driven, variable and fixed dose) and Shaily Harmony.
\- Gland Pharma: Gland fills cartridges with the API supplied by its pharma partners for three GLP-1 products namely liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide

text: Brazil Market Formation (2026): Semaglutide's LOE Sets the Stage for Formal Market Expansion

Current State Pre-Generic Entry: GLP-1 access remains constrained primarily by affordability. Brazil's GLP-1 market remains materially underpenetrated, not because of weak demand, but because affordability continues to cap adoption in an almost entirely out-of-pocket market. Monthly treatment costs for leading GLP-1 therapies still range from roughly R\$800 to R\$1,600 (US\$160 to US\$320 per month), levels that restrict access to a narrow upper-income tier and keep penetration well below the market's underlying clinical potential. The scale of demand for compounded alternatives and unauthorized imports further supports this affordability bottleneck, suggesting that many patients are actively seeking lower-cost access outside the formal market rather than opting out of treatment altogether. Supply constraints appear less broad-based today, though availability remains inconsistent for Mounjaro/tirzepatide, where recurring stockouts can still limit realized volumes even within the high-income addressable group. As a result, Brazil currently has only \~2.1mn active GLP-1 users by our 1Q26 estimates (1.3% of the current adult population), underscoring the large pool of unmet demand in a sizeable emerging market where category penetration remains well below potential.

Early pricing moves suggest incumbents are already preparing for semaglutide competition. We have also seen some initial discounts and price reductions on semaglutide's authorized generic from Eurofarma, see LatAm Healthcare: GLP-1 Brazil Tracker: April Imports Remain Solid Despite MoM Decline; New ANVISA Data Adds Insights (7 May 2026). These moves are still immaterial to overall market dynamics, as price points remain too high to materially broaden access or trigger a meaningful shift in category penetration. However, they are directionally important: the early discounting suggests that the Novo Nordisk-Eurofarma partnership is already preparing for incoming competition ahead of broader semaglutide generic entry, with pricing likely to become a more relevant competitive lever as additional approved alternatives reach the market.

Generic-led transition in 2026: the beginning of the price reset and accelerating adoption. Following the expected entry of semaglutide generics in 2H26, we forecast a marked expansion in GLP-1 access as affordability improves, though the market may take time beyond 2026 to reach its post-LOE equilibrium. Semaglutide generics have been delayed, with the first approval (for EMS product) granted in May 2026 with a launch planned for June 15th; we are therefore modeling market formation in 2H26; see LatAm Healthcare & Education: Our takes from Brazil Journal HC Conference (28 Apr 2026). Once the first branded generics launch, semaglutide prices should begin to step down, with our forecast for semaglutide generics reaching \~R\$687/month (US\$137/month) by YE26, from \~R\$1k/month (US\$200/month) currently for Novo's offering (Ozempic and Wegovy). We estimate total GLP-1 market sales of \~R\$14.3bn (US\$2.5bn) in 2026, with active users rising to \~3.4mn by YE26, as lower entry prices allow volumes to better reflect underlying demand. That said, 2026 should still be viewed as an acceleration year rather than a steady state, with additional entrants, ongoing price compression, and broader affordability gains likely to play out gradually through late-2026, leaving penetration still below long-term potential by year-end.

Post-LOE Shift: semaglutide generics unlock a step-change in access and market stabilization. Beyond the initial 2026 adjustment, semaglutide's loss of exclusivity may drive a structural shift in Brazil's GLP-1 market, as lower prices unlock a significantly broader addressable population in a country with steep income distribution. We expect the entry of multiple generics to result in a cumulative \~70% reduction in monthly treatment costs, with semaglutide reaching R\$294/month (US\$59/month) post-LOE (see Exhibit 28). At this price point, affordability expands meaningfully into middle-income households, shifting GLP-1 access from a high-income niche toward a broader mass-market therapy. We estimate that the addressable GLP-1 population expands to \~17mn potential users post-LOE (see Exhibit 29), with Mounjaro and future Lilly offerings likely concentrated in higher-income cohorts, while semaglutide becomes the preferred option across Brazil's large B2-C income classes. As adoption broadens, we expect the GLP-1 market to continue scaling after 2026, reaching \~R\$20.6bn (US\$3.4bn) in 2027, \~R \$30.9bn (US\$4.3bn) in 2029, and stabilizing around a long-term opportunity of \~R\$39bn (US\$5.1bn), driven primarily by price elasticity and stronger consumer willingness to pay, rather than changes in underlying obesity prevalence (see Exhibit 30).

text: Local producer likely to be the main beneficiary of LOE. The post-LOE semaglutide market should be shaped by partnerships between global generic producers, mostly from

India and China, and local players. Within this landscape, EMS, a non-listed family-owned company, stands out as the only domestic producer and likely the best positioned to benefit from semaglutide's LOE, with its synthetic semaglutide pen, Ozivy, becoming the first to receive Anvisa approval on May 26 (see here, Portuguese only). The company has invested in local GLP-1 manufacturing capacity, with reported annual capacity of approximately 20mn injectable pens for liraglutide and semaglutide. In our view, this local footprint could give EMS a cost advantage, as it does not rely on royalty-bearing partnerships with foreign manufacturers. The Brazilian government's decision to reduce the import tariff on components used in EMS's injectable pens from 14.4% to 0% for one year on March 26, with a quota of up to 30mn units, should further support competitive pricing as production scales. Following approval, CMED set the ceiling price at levels comparable to Ozempic; however, EMS announced a retail price of BRL 452, with the potential to reach BRL 287 (US\$57) for a three-month period under the company's discount program (see here, Portuguese only). Looking ahead, should EMS successfully scale production, it could broaden access through formal channels and position itself as the leading low-cost producer in the post-LOE semaglutide segment.

Potential new entrants: a broader competitive pipeline beyond EMS. While EMS is the first mover following Ozivy's Anvisa approval, the post-LOE semaglutide market should become increasingly crowded as additional players move through the regulatory pipeline. According to G1 (see here, portuguese only), Anvisa had 17 semaglutide-related filings in progress, including 8 already under analysis, of which 3 were in an advanced stage awaiting company responses to Anvisa's technical questions. With EMS now approved, we believe one of these advanced files was likely Ozivy, but the broader pipeline remains meaningful. Among those names, public reporting points to potential contenders including Hypera, Biomm, through its agreement with Biocon, as well as Cimed, Prati-Donaduzzi (see here, portuguese only) and potentially Sandoz, which has reportedly identified Brazil as one of its early 2026 target markets for generic semaglutide (see here). In our view, EMS may capture the initial first-mover advantage, but the medium-term market structure should evolve toward a multi-player branded semaglutide-copy landscape, with competition driven by approval timing, CMED pricing, pen supply, local distribution reach, physician relationships and the ability to fund patient discount programs.
Implications for Novo Nordisk post-LOE: Brazil as an early test case for ex-US erosion.

Brazil is one of Novo Nordisk's first large emerging-market tests of post-LOE semaglutide dynamics, and the recent approval of EMS's Ozivy suggests the generic approval cycle is now beginning to move. While the delayed approval process gave Novo more time to defend its franchise, the structural risk is now becoming more tangible: as approved synthetic semaglutide products reach the market, Novo is likely to face price erosion, volume share dilution and increased competition from local players with strong distribution, prescribing relationships and retail reach. The key debate is how much of the expanding market Novo can retain as semaglutide access broadens from a premium niche toward a more mass-market therapy. In our view, Brazil should be watched as an early indicator of Novo's broader ex-US LOE headwinds, particularly in markets where affordability constraints are high, local generic capabilities are strong and demand is already visible through informal and compounding-pharmacy channels.

Impacts on our coverage: Semaglutide's LOE should be positive for both RADL (OW) and HYPE (OW), though through different mechanisms. For RADL, the main upside is the expansion of the addressable market as lower semaglutide prices move GLP-1 access beyond a narrow high-income niche, alongside the migration of demand currently served by unauthorized imports and compounded alternatives into the formal pharmacy channel. While lower prices may pressure average ticket, elasticity should support higher volumes, traffic and recurring prescription demand, with RADL well positioned to capture this shift given its national footprint, digital capabilities, supplier relationships and ability to sell both branded and generic GLP-1s. For HYPE, the opportunity is more execution-dependent, but potentially meaningful: if the company secures timely Anvisa approval and launches in the early waves of branded semaglutide copies, it could participate directly in the expansion and formalization of a market where demand already exists but is still partly priced out of the legal channel. EMS's first-mover advantage and local manufacturing footprint are relevant competitive hurdles, but the market should evolve into a multi-player branded-copy segment, where HYPE's physician relationships, marketing capabilities, retail reach and brand-building capacity could support share gains as semaglutide shifts from a premium niche into a broader mass-market therapy.

Risks to our estimates: unauthorized imports and compounded GLP-1s highlight unmet demand, but also regulatory and safety risk. The emergence of compounded, informal, and cross-border GLP-1 channels is another signal that underlying demand exceeds the formal market's current affordability curve. Before generic entry, there was an expectation that lower-cost alternatives would reduce average prices and expand access, but the size of the parallel market suggests that demand among lower-income consumers already exists, even before formal semaglutide generics have arrived. For reference, according to RADL's 1Q26 conference call, the unofficial GLP-1 market could be around 3-4x the size of the official market. Going forward, a key catalyst would be tighter enforcement on unauthorized imports and compounded alternatives, which could pressure black-market supply, while lower prices from approved generics should encourage consumers to transition into the legal market.
Although China's GLP-1 market is much smaller than the US, it possesses significant peptide API capacity, the result of a serendipitous set of conditions.

China's current GLP-1 market is small compared to the US market: In 2025, the total GLP-1 market in China was only Rmb8.1bn (\~US\$1.1bn), growing 27% YoY. Close to 90% of the market came from semaglutide (IQVIA), a fraction of the US market in 2025 (US\$52bn [also from IQVIA], up 37% YoY). Part of the explanation lies in later approval dates for the branded drugs and a low level of reimbursement status. Of the 10 GLP-1 brands launched since 2010 in China, most launches lagged the US by several years including Ozempic (3.5 years) and Wegovy (3 years), with Mounjaro launched for diabetes 2 years after the US.

text: The grey/unofficial channel in China is significant. This market consists of online sales, counterfeit products, and sales of raw APIs. Chinese authorities have intensified crackdowns on unlicensed production and sales of GLP-1s in recent months; for example, beginning mid-May, pharmacies require hospital paper prescriptions from customers in order to dispense GLP-1 drugs. Although the official market in China is small, a significant portion of the addressable market has so far leaked through unofficial channels.

New launches from Lilly, supported by local CDMOs, could help drive market growth before generic entry. Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) was just included into the NRDL earlier this year, so volume would likely expand this year (with a price concession). Upcoming launch of Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo (orforglipron), could also drive uptake with a differentiated convenience. In early 2026, Lilly partnered with Chinese CDMO Pharmaron to supply Foundayo (note); we note that Pharmaron's oral solids facility in Beijing has an annual capacity of 1-2bn tablets. The site could potentially be dedicated to the drug, which suggests significant market potential (note). Leading Chinese CDMO WuXi AppTec has also been a long-standing global partner of Lilly's.

The patent for semaglutide expired in China in March 2026. The compound patent for semaglutide was filed in March 2006; and was set to expire in China March 2026 under the 20-year patent term set by the WTO, earlier than in the US and EU where Novo leveraged specific patent term extension mechanisms. No such mechanism existed in China prior to June 2021, when the government introduced a similar extension mechanism modeled on US/EU's. Semaglutide (Ozempic) was first approved in China in April, 2021 for the diabetes indication, thus narrowly missing the enactment of the extension pathway.

However, the exclusivity is extended potentially until April 2027 under the China-Switzerland Free Trade Agreement (CSFTA). Novo received approval for semaglutide in April 2021 in China through a filing was via its Swiss-registered entity, Novo Nordisk Pharma AG. In 2014, China and Switzerland signed the CSFTA, a bilateral economic treaty that reduces trade barriers, improves market access, and strengthens IP protection. For the latter, the two countries grant six years of market protection for undisclosed pharmaceutical test data, counting from the drug's approval date (i.e. April 2021 for semaglutide in China). When the patent expired in March 2026, Novo invoked this specific clause, barring generic launches in China until April 2027. Due to this clause, generic applicants cannot use Novo's trial data in their regulatory submissions till then. Hangzhou
Jiuyuan challenged the CSFTA in the Zhejiang Provincial court in January 2026; but at time of writing, no generic has been approved in China.

In anticipation of semaglutide's patent expiry, a host of Chinese developers have geared up applications for a biosimilar. These include major pharma companies like Fosun and Sino Biopharm (Chia Tai), and specialty companies (either in diabetes or in insulins/peptides) like United Labs and Huadong. Most applications in the queue are for the diabetes indication. One of the frontrunners in this race, Huadong, indicated at its end-May shareholders meeting that because of CSFTA, its semaglutide generic would not launch until after April 2027, thus confirming the validity of the extension. Meanwhile, Hybio has also recently submitted a biosimilar application (co-developed with CR Double-Crane) and is expected to serve as the API supplier.

text: We recently updated our views on the evolving GLP-1 landscape across obesity and T2D, refreshing our global obesity model and latest GLP-1 assumptions (see "Tracking the GLP-1 'Unlock' HERE). We continue to see sustained uptake of GLP-1 therapies and believe five key drivers can support further global penetration over time: (1) the launch of oral GLP-1 therapies (Novo's Wegovy pill and LLY's Foundayo), (2) broader access to all GLP-1's in the US for elderly patients via Medicare (at a co-pay of \$50/month), (3) international market expansion (such as China and Brazil, which we discuss in detail), (4) next-generation molecules/pathways, and (5) clinical benefits in new disease areas such as inflammation and neurological indications.

We believe orals, such as Novo's oral Wegovy pill (oral peptide GLP-1, approved on December 22, 2025 for obesity) and LLY's Foundayo (oral small molecule GLP-1, approved on April 1, 2026 for obesity) will also drive the next inflection in the obesity market. On 4Q25 EPS LLY reiterated its view that the entry of oral GLP-1's will expand the market, which was also supported by Novo's 4Q25 earnings call commentary that most oral Wegovy patients are incretin naïve. In our recent AlphaWise consumer survey, 77% of respondents on the Wegovy pill are new to GLP-1 therapy, further supporting our view that orals will substantially expand the category (LINK). On 1Q26 LLY noted that the significant inventory build speaks to upcoming international roll out of the drug as they see a "huge" opportunity for Foundayo around the world, also consistent with our view (LINK).

Oral GLP-1 therapies in development aim to deliver the benefits of existing injectable agents while offering patients an alternative formulation and, in some cases, improved scalability on a global basis. A key scientific challenge is that most incretins are peptides that are rapidly degraded in the stomach, leading companies to pursue either (1) engineering oral peptide delivery systems, such as Novo's SNAC delivery platform utilized in Rybelsus/Ozempic pill and Wegovy pill, or (2) non-peptide small molecules, such as LLY's Foundayo. Oral peptide formulations typically require food and water restrictions (e.g., administration on an empty stomach followed by a waiting period before eating, drinking, or taking other medications) to facilitate absorption. Taken together with manufacturing considerations, we believe non-peptide small molecules may ultimately prove both more scalable and more convenient. As a result, we see LLY's Foundayo playing an important role in OUS markets over time, while noting that Novo's oral Wegovy may face drug-substance scaling constraints as demand expands.
We model Foundayo 2026/2035 sales of \$1.4bn/\$29bn vs. VA cons' of \$1.3bn/\$27bn.

Generic GLP-1s worth watching for Drug Packaging names
We view the launch of GLP-1 generics as incremental growth opportunities for drug packaging names such as WST and STVN. Both WST and STVN have a strong presence in GLP-1 injectables. Notably:

list_items: - GLP-1 represents approximately 18% of WST's total company revenue, with \~10% in elastomer components and \~8% in West Vantage (contract manufacturing).
WST's portfolio participates across multiple modalities with vials, prefilled syringes, auto-injectors, and pens using WST's elastomer components.
Approximately 90% of WST's GLP-1 exposure is from branded products and 10% from generics.
- GLP-1 represents 19-20% of STVN's total company revenue. Key products within STVN's portfolio serving the GLP market include the company's Nexa syringes and EZ-fill cartridges for multi-dose pens.

text: Minimal trade down expected from GLP-1 generics. Both WST and STVN primarily serve the GLP-1 market through products in their high value portfolios. Compared to products in their standard portfolios, high value products come with higher ASPs and better margin profiles. Per our conversations with management, both WST and STVN expect minimal trade down from branded GLP-1s to generics. We see generic manufacturers adopting similar high value primary packaging specifications used by branded originators in their Drug Master Files to reduce regulatory risk, allowing WST and STVN to continue supplying their most profitable products from their high value portfolio, and allowing for meaningful top line flow through to the EPS line.

GLP-1 generics could provide ASP tailwind from lesser volume discounts. Entrenched in their business models, both WST and STVN generally provide volume discounts to large customers. Using the same assumptions for GLP-1 patient pool expansion for STVN, we found generic GLP-1s could drive 70-120 bps of incremental growth. Novo Nordisk (EW): We expect Novo Nordisk to be under pressure in post-LOE

markets. We expect Canada to be the bellwether for future developed market dynamics over coming years; specifically, the extent to which price and volume competition in the semaglutide franchise leads to an erosion of Novo's Wegovy/Ozempic sales. We see some scope for Novo to partially compensate through its Wegovy Pill and through innovation. On Wegovy Pill, script trends in the US YTD have been encouraging (although we are waiting to see prescriptions trends holding through the summer and escalation to highest doses) but we believe the API requirement will limit Novo's ability execute on a broad ex-US launch (unlike LLY with Foundayo). On innovation, CagriSema (GLP-1/amylin) launch in 2027 will be a first step to partially protect the franchise in the US, but we see more potential from the cagrilintide mono (amylin, potential launch in 2028), zenagamtide/amycretin subcut (GLP-1/amylin 2029-2030) and more importantly zenagamtide oral (2030), which carries the highest differentiation potential in our view. At this stage, we see less potential for Novo's triple agonists which will only come to market next decade and 5+ years after Lilly's retatrutide. Therefore, with key new launches skewed to 2028-2030+, we see a risk for Novo's diabetes/obesity franchise to struggle between inexpensive semglutide generics and innovation from Lilly and other branded players, and we see consensus' forecasts for \$23bn sales for semaglutide in 2033 as likely at risk (MSe \$16bn).
Eli Lilly (OW): We expect Eli Lilly's franchise to be more insulated from generic

pressure given: (1) Differentiation of Mounjaro (GLP-GIP) vs. Semaglutide (GLP) based on head-to-head Ph3 data in obesity and T2D, (2) a portfolio of pipeline drugs with novel mechanisms of action such as Retatrutide (GLP-GIP-glucagon) and Eloralintide (selective amylin), and (3) a scalable oral GLP-1 pill in Foundayo. We model LLY incretin franchise sales growing from \$60bn in 2026 to \$101bn in 2035.

Dr Reddy's (EW): Dr. Reddy's is an early entrant in generic semaglutide in Canada, India and other markets with in-house API production and partner-led pen manufacturing/fill-and-finish. It is rapidly expanding capacity (targeting >40mn pens by FY28 vs. 6–7mn in 2026) and pursuing global markets, including established GLP-1 market like Canada. The company is positioning itself as a scaled, globally focused generics player, leveraging cost leadership, integrated manufacturing, and supply chain control to gain market share.

Divi's Labs (OW): The company aims to be one of the largest players in peptides globally, and currently has the largest Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis (SPPS) scale (i.e. multiple \~3,000L reactors) in India. Management confirmed that the company is involved in manufacturing amino acids and fragments for the API of several MNCs GLP-1 projects, including innovative drugs. We therefore see Divi's Labs as a potential beneficiary of volume expansion in the GLP-1 market through exposure to API manufacturing.

Sandoz (UW): Sandoz is expecting to launch a generic semaglutide in Canada and Brazil in the second half of 2026, and is targeting other markets such as Mexico in 2027 ahead of the EU and US LOE in the early/mid-2030s. The company is partnering for both API and fill-and-finish for the first markets, and will make a decision on investing in API and F&F capacity based on the market dynamics in the first LOE markets. We currently model a limited contribution from GLP-1 in 2027 in our model based on the Canada and Brazil opportunity; if Sandoz emerges as a market share leader in Canada and Brazil and prices stabilise at an acceptable level, there could be upside to our numbers from GLP-1 generics, in particular if Sandoz decides to invest in F&F manufacturing to address the US and European markets. We currently expect \~US\$100-120mn sales by 2030 for Sandoz Ozempic generics in Canada (implying 15-20% share of the Ozempic generic market in Canada).

Medtide (3880.HK, EW): One of a handful of Chinese semaglutide API suppliers on the US FDA's Green List of importers, Medtide possesses ton-scale capacity. However, it is a peptides and oligos focused CDMO that serves novel drug contracts. So far, it has not announced plans to capture the semaglutide biosimilars market, as opposed to Hybio Pharma (300199.SZ, not covered) and Jiangsu Sinopep (688076.SH, not covered) which are dedicated semaglutide API suppliers.

United Labs (3933.HK, EW): One of the first filers for a semaglutide biosimilar in China. As a well-established insulin player in China, it has the sales network to push other products from its diabesity pipeline. Novo licensed the ex-China rights to United Labs' triple agonist UBT251 (GLP-1/GIP/glucagon) in 2025 (trial progress).

Hypera (OW): The opportunity for Hypera in Brazil from a generic semaglutide launch is execution-dependent, but potentially meaningful: if the company secures timely Anvisa approval and launches in the early waves of branded semaglutide copies, it could participate directly in the expansion and formalization of a market where demand already exists but is still partly priced out of the legal channel. EMS's first-mover advantage and local manufacturing footprint are relevant competitive hurdles, but the market should evolve into a multi-player branded-copy segment, where HYPE's physician relationships, marketing capabilities, retail reach and brand-building capacity could support share gains as semaglutide shifts from a premium niche into a broader mass-market therapy.

Raia Drogasil (OW): We see upside in the expansion of the addressable market in Brazil as lower semaglutide prices move GLP-1 access beyond a narrow high-income niche, alongside the migration of demand currently served by unauthorized imports and compounded alternatives into the formal pharmacy channel. While lower prices may pressure average ticket, elasticity should support higher volumes, traffic and recurring prescription demand, with RADL well positioned to capture this shift given its national footprint, digital capabilities, supplier relationships and ability to sell both branded and generic GLP-1s.

West Pharmaceutical Services (EW): We believe generic GLP-1s will be an incremental growth driver for WST and estimate it could drive 30-50 bps of annual growth through 2030. We expect minimal product trade down from branded to generic GLP-1s, enabling WST to serve the generics GLP-1s market with its high value portfolio, which should drive meaningful topline flow through to the EPS line. In addition we see the potential for ASP upside from lesser volume discounts as generics players will not be able to receive the same level of volume discounts compared to the two main branded GLP-1 players.

Stevanato Group (EW): We see STVN benefiting from generic GLP-1s for the same aforementioned reasons as WST. However with 19-20% company exposure to GLP-1s, we expect STVN will benefit to a even greater degree.
